chokepoints.name: Strait of Hormuz
chokepoints.why_it_matters: Flow control over an estimated ~21 million barrels per day of crude oil and condensate — roughly a fifth of global supply.

countries_most_exposed.reason: Major buyer of Gulf crude oil, shipped through Hormuz then Malacca.
Major buyer of Gulf crude oil, including from Iraq and Saudi Arabia.
>80% crude dependency on Gulf exporters per unified research estimate; near-zero domestic geological substitutes.
>80% crude dependency on Gulf exporters; strategic reserves cover roughly 90-120 days.

countries_with_leverage.leverage: high — northern coastal control via anti-ship batteries, fast-attack craft, and island bases (Abu Musa, the Tunbs)
countries_with_leverage.caveat: Iran has repeatedly threatened closure during periods of tension but has never actually sustained a full closure — Oman shares southern-shore control and global naval powers (notably the US Fifth Fleet, based in Bahrain) actively deter unilateral closure.

chokepoints.alternative_routes: Saudi East-West Petroline (~5M bpd capacity) and UAE's Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline/ADCOP (~1.5M bpd) allow some crude to bypass Hormuz entirely — a real but partial mitigation, covering a minority of total Gulf export volume.
chokepoints.source: EIA Monthly Energy Review 2025-2026, via user-provided unified research

active_crisis_2026.statement: Since the 2026 Iran War began (28 Feb 2026), the Strait of Hormuz has seen repeated real disruption — Iran has fired on commercial vessels (e.g. 6-7 Jul 2026) and asserted fee-collection/routing control attempts, testing the limits of an Apr-Jul 2026 ceasefire memorandum. This is no longer a purely hypothetical chokepoint risk for this conflict — it is an active, ongoing crisis.
active_crisis_2026.confidence: high — verified via live sources (Britannica, Wikipedia), September 2026

chokepoints.name: Strait of Malacca
chokepoints.why_it_matters: Chokepoint for an estimated ~16 million barrels/day of crude oil and roughly 60% of China's maritime trade flows. Named the 'Malacca Dilemma' by Chinese leadership (Hu Jintao, 2003) precisely because of this dependency.

countries_most_exposed.reason: ~72% of China's crude oil imports transit this route per the unified research estimate (a commonly cited range is 70-85% depending on year/source); no comparable-scale alternative exists.
Heavily energy-import-dependent economy relying on Gulf oil shipped through this route.
Near-total energy import dependence, similar route reliance to Japan.

countries_with_leverage.leverage: moderate — geographic proximity, not a blockade capability
countries_with_leverage.reason: India's Andaman & Nicobar Command sits at the northern approach, commanding the Six Degree, Eight Degree, and Nine Degree Channels near the strait's entrance — a genuine forward position for surveillance and, in a severe crisis, interdiction risk.
countries_with_leverage.caveat: The strait itself is legally administered under UNCLOS transit-passage rules by Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore — not India. India's leverage is proximity-based deterrence and surveillance, not sovereign control, and a full blockade would be an act of war against global shipping broadly, not a targeted move against one country.

chokepoints.alternative_routes: Sunda Strait and Lombok-Makassar Strait (Indonesia) can absorb rerouted traffic, particularly deep-draft vessels — at the cost of an additional 3-5 shipping days and higher fuel costs.
chokepoints.source: IEA World Energy Outlook & Critical Minerals Market Review 2025/2026, via user-provided unified research

chokepoints.name: Turkish Straits (Bosphorus / Dardanelles)
chokepoints.location: Türkiye, connecting the Black Sea to the Mediterranean
chokepoints.why_it_matters: Sole natural maritime passage between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean — controls all Black Sea naval ingress/egress.

countries_most_exposed.reason: Black Sea Fleet's only route to the Mediterranean/open ocean.

countries_with_leverage.leverage: very high — full legal and physical control
countries_with_leverage.reason: Administered under the 1936 Montreux Convention; Türkiye regulates naval and commercial transit and has invoked Article 19 (restricting non-riparian warship transit during wartime) during the Russia-Ukraine war (2022-2026).

chokepoints.alternative_routes: None — this is the sole natural maritime passage from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean.
chokepoints.source: IISS Military Balance 2026, via user-provided unified research

chokepoints.name: Bab el-Mandeb
chokepoints.location: Between Yemen and Djibouti/Eritrea, gateway to the Red Sea and Suez Canal
chokepoints.why_it_matters: Gateway to the Red Sea and Suez Canal; disruption here forces rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope.

countries_most_exposed.reason: A meaningful share of China-Europe container traffic transits this route via Suez.

countries_with_leverage.leverage: high but asymmetric — interdiction, not sovereign control
countries_with_leverage.reason: Demonstrated capability to threaten shipping via anti-ship ballistic/cruise missiles and drones (2023-2026 Red Sea shipping disruptions).
countries_with_leverage.caveat: This is asymmetric interdiction by a non-state armed actor, not a government exercising legal chokepoint control — a materially different kind of leverage than Türkiye's at the Turkish Straits.

chokepoints.alternative_routes: Cape of Good Hope detour — adds an estimated 10-14 days transit time and a significant freight cost increase (commonly cited estimates cluster around 30%, though this varies by route and vessel).
chokepoints.source: WTO Global Trade Outlook and Statistics 2026, via user-provided unified research

chokepoints.name: Andaman & Nicobar Islands approach
chokepoints.location: India, at the eastern approach to the Bay of Bengal / northern Strait of Malacca
chokepoints.why_it_matters: Forward surveillance and potential interdiction position over the Six Degree and Ten Degree Channels — the northern approach to the Malacca Strait.

countries_most_exposed.reason: See CHOKEPOINT_MALACCA — this entry is India's specific asset enabling leverage there, not a separate dependency.

countries_with_leverage.leverage: moderate — surveillance and interdiction-risk, not sovereign strait control
countries_with_leverage.reason: India's only tri-service unified military command (Andaman & Nicobar Command, headquartered at Port Blair) operates deep surveillance of the Six Degree and Ten Degree Channels in the eastern Bay of Bengal.

chokepoints.alternative_routes: A vessel could reroute south of Sumatra into the Lombok/Ombai-Wetar straits to avoid the immediate ANC surveillance zone, at a cost in transit time.
chokepoints.source: IISS Military Balance 2026, via user-provided unified research

chokepoints.name: Sunda / Lombok Straits
chokepoints.why_it_matters: Deep-water bypass routes for ultra-large crude carriers and submarines that cannot transit the shallower Malacca Strait.

countries_most_exposed.reason: Alternative route if Malacca is disrupted, so relevant to China's contingency planning specifically.

countries_with_leverage.reason: Complete physical control within Indonesian Archipelagic Waters under Indonesia's declared Archipelagic Sea Lanes (ASL).

chokepoints.alternative_routes: Long-distance open Pacific transit, or the shallower Torres Strait as a less practical alternative.
chokepoints.source: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 / user-provided unified research

chokepoints.name: GIUK Gap (Greenland-Iceland-UK)
chokepoints.why_it_matters: Chokepoint for Russian Northern Fleet nuclear and attack submarines attempting to break into the North Atlantic.

countries_most_exposed.reason: Northern Fleet egress to the open Atlantic is constrained by NATO monitoring here.

countries_with_leverage.leverage: high, as part of a NATO multilateral effort
countries_with_leverage.reason: SOSUS/IUSS undersea acoustic sensor arrays plus P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft provide persistent NATO monitoring of this gap, in cooperation with Norway, Iceland, and the US.

chokepoints.alternative_routes: Arctic trans-polar under-ice transit — technically possible for submarines but operationally specialized and monitored by its own dedicated sensor networks.
chokepoints.source: IISS Military Balance 2026, via user-provided unified research
